From its constitution and stakeholder consultations to employee demands and the fitment factor debate, here are five key developments and what central government employees and pensioners can expect on salary and pension revision. Kirti Jha Published 3 Nov 2026, 06:53 PM IST Prefer Livemint on Google The commission also opened a separate questionnaire exercise through the MyGov platform on 5 February 2026. (AI-generated image used for representational purpose.) AI Quick Read The 8th Central Pay Commission (CPC) completes one year on 3 November 2026, but central government employees and pensioners are still waiting for clarity on revised salaries, the fitment factor and pension increases. While the commission has invited representations from employee associations and pensioners and begun stakeholder consultations, it has not yet submitted its recommendations to the government. The commission was formally constituted through a government notification on 3 November 2025, after the Union Cabinet approved its Terms of Reference (ToR) on 28 October 2025. It has been given 18 months from the date of its constitution to submit its recommendations, putting the expected deadline around May 2027. For employees and pensioners, three monetary issues remain particularly important: the fitment factor and revised basic salary, pension revision and the effective date of implementation. Here are three key developments in the 8th Pay Commission's journey so far. 1. 8th Pay Commission fitment factor and minimum basic salary remain undecided The fitment factor is among the biggest concerns for central government employees because it will determine how their existing basic pay is converted into revised basic pay under the 8th Pay Commission. However, the government has not announced an official fitment factor or revised minimum basic salary yet. In a written reply to the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026, the Finance Ministry clarified that the 8th Pay Commission had not submitted its recommendations to the government. Under the 7th Pay Commission, a fitment factor of 2.57 was applied, taking the minimum basic pay from ₹ 7,000 to ₹ 18,000. Employees are now awaiting clarity on whether the 8th CPC will recommend a higher fitment factor and how this will affect their revised salaries. The final fitment factor and revised pay structure will depend on the commission's recommendations and the government's decision. 2. Pension revision for central government pensioners is also pending The 8th Pay Commission's mandate covers retirement benefits, including pension-related matters. Its recommendations will therefore have implications not only for serving central government employees but also for existing pensioners. Pensioners are awaiting clarity on revised basic pension, family pension and the methodology that will be used to calculate their revised retirement benefits. The fitment factor will also be important for pension revision, as the commission's recommendations will determine the framework for revising pay and pension. However, no official pension revision formula or revised pension amount has been announced so far. The Cabinet-approved Terms of Reference require the commission to consider the financial implications of its recommendations, including the unfunded cost of non-contributory pension schemes and the government's fiscal position. Therefore, pensioners will have to wait for the commission's recommendations and the government's subsequent decision before revised pension amounts can be confirmed. 3. Will revised salary and pension be effective from 1 January 2026? Another important question for employees and pensioners is when the revised salary and pension will come into effect. The government's 28 October 2025 press release stated that, following the usual 10-year cycle of Pay Commissions, the effect of the 8th CPC recommendations would normally be expected from 1 January 2026. However, this is not the same as a formal implementation order. In its Lok Sabha reply on 10 August 2026, the Finance Ministry said that the commission had not yet submitted its recommendations. The government has therefore not confirmed the final implementation date or the fitment factor. The commission has 18 months from its constitution on 3 November 2025 to submit its recommendations. This puts the deadline around May 2027, although it can submit interim reports if recommendations on particular matters are finalised earlier. If the government subsequently approves a retrospective effective date, employees and pensioners could become eligible for arrears for the applicable period. However, the payment timeline and arrears calculation will depend on the final government notification. For now, employees and pensioners should not treat 1 January 2026 as a confirmed payment or implementation date. What should employees and pensioners expect next? The next major milestone will be the submission of the 8th Pay Commission's recommendations, expected around May 2027. The report will provide the framework for revised basic pay, the fitment factor, pension revision and other retirement benefits. The government will then examine the recommendations and decide which proposals to accept before issuing implementation orders. For central government employees, the key questions remain how much their basic salary will increase and what fitment factor will be adopted. For pensioners, the focus will be on revised basic pension and family pension. One year after its constitution, the 8th Pay Commission has yet to announce the monetary changes that employees and pensioners are waiting for. The fitment factor, revised salary structure, pension formula and implementation timeline all remain subject to the commission's recommendations and the government's final decision. Her reporting focuses on helping readers understand complex financial developments through data-driven, research-backed stories that explain how policy changes, market trends and regulatory decisions affect investors and households.

Before joining Mint, Kirti worked at ET Money, where she specialised in mutual fund research and investment analysis. She tracked portfolio disclosures, fund manager strategies, sectoral allocation shifts and investment trends, distilling large datasets into investor-focused insights. Her work combined quantitative analysis with consumer-centric storytelling, enabling readers to better understand fund positioning, portfolio changes and long-term investment opportunities.

Kirti holds a Bachelor's degree in Economics from Indraprastha College for Women, University of Delhi, and a Master's in Finance from the Jindal School of Banking & Finance at O.P. Jindal Global University. Her academic training emphasised analytical thinking, quantitative research and financial decision-making, providing a strong foundation in understanding capital markets, financial systems and economic policy. With a combined experience in investment research and financial journalism, she is committed to producing accurate, accessible and insightful journalism that empowers readers to make well-informed financial decisions.
